newsitem.title: USA: Clinton back to raising money for Democrats.
newsitem.headline: Clinton back to raising money for Democrats.

text.p: Hours after President Bill Clinton faced tough questions about how he and fellow Democrats financed their 1996 campaigns, he was in a familiar setting -- at another Democratic Party fund-raiser.

This one on Tuesday night raised nearly $1 million for the party from a fund-raising arm called the Democratic Business Council. About 70 people paid a minimum of $10,000 each to attend the salmon-and-rice dinner event, meaning that less than three months after the Nov. 5 elections, the parties are reloading for their next battles.

In his remarks to the group in a chandeliered ballroom at a downtown hotel, Clinton alluded to the grilling he received on Tuesday afternoon at a White House news conference about ongoing questions on campaign fund-raising that have shadowed the early days of his second term. Nine out of 22 questions were devoted to the topic.

"They said, well, does it set a good example that you're going to this fund-raiser tonight, and I said, yes, I think it does," Clinton said, going on to stress that no campaign finance reform proposal under consideration by Congress would use taxpayer money to completely fund the political parties.
"So we have to depend upon people to help us," he said.
But he insisted that he had never made any policy decision based on how it would help financial contributors.
"I never had anyone in four years who asked me to make a decision as president based on being a financial contributor, and I have never made such a decision," he said.

Clinton insists no laws were broken in the way Democrats attracted donors. But there have been so many questions raised that Republicans on Capitol Hill are promising oversight hearings and want Clinton to appoint an independent counsel to investigate.

FBI Director Louis Freeh said a 25-agent FBI task force has been assigned to investigate activities involving former Democratic fund-raiser John Huang, who tapped Asian-American sources for about $2.5 million, and about $1.5 million was returned because of questions as to whether it came from foreign sources, which would be illegal.

Beyond that, questions have been raised about Clinton's White House coffee chats held with wealthy people who afterward contributed large sums to the Democrats -- a reported total of $27 million. Big donors have stayed overnight in the Lincoln Bedroom.

A new evolving story line is whether contributors were granted a "day at the White House," free to use the tennis court, swimming pool and bowling alley for donating or raising $250,000. By the same token, Republicans are said to have given donors a season ticket of access to Capitol Hill for $250,000.

"The people who were there on the day in question were not charged a fee," Clinton told his news conference. "Some of them were our contributors. They had raised money for me in the past. Some of them had not. And so I don't think it's quite an accurate characterisation."
He also said the problem with the system now is that it takes huge sums to run a credible campaign. He said this is why campaign finance reform is so badly needed.
"Nobody is blameless here. It costs so much money to pay for these campaigns that mistakes were made by people who either did it deliberately or inadvertently," Clinton said.
The chief Senate investigator of campaign finance improprieties promised on Tuesday to run a fair and even-handed inquiry of activities of both Democrats and Republicans.
"Our work will include any improper activities by Republicans, Democrats or other political partisans," Sen. Fred Thompson, chairman of the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, told the Senate.
